stem: Which pair of pills builds a bar chart?

options.text: `Minutes Watched` on Columns and `Sessions (Count)` on Rows
options.rationale: Two measures, one per shelf, make a scatterplot, not bars.

options.text: Continuous `MONTH(Start)` on Columns and `Minutes Watched` on Rows
options.rationale: A date with a measure draws a line under Automatic.

options.text: `Genre` on Rows and `Minutes Watched` on Columns
options.rationale: A dimension and a measure on the two shelves is the bar chart recipe; Automatic then picks the Bar mark.

options.text: `Genre` on Rows and `Device` on Columns, with nothing on the Marks card
options.rationale: Two dimensions and no measure give a table of headers, not bars.

explanation: A bar chart needs a dimension on one of Rows or Columns and a measure on the other. The dimension supplies the headers, and the measure supplies the axis along which the bars grow.

stem: Driftlight wants to show which genres people watch most. Which chart fits best?

options.text: A sorted horizontal bar chart of `Minutes Watched` by `Genre`
options.rationale: Comparing one measure across the members of a dimension is the job of a bar chart.

options.text: A scatterplot with `Genre` on Columns and `Genre` on Rows
options.rationale: Scatterplots plot a measure against a measure; a dimension on each shelf only builds headers.

options.text: A line chart of `Minutes Watched` over continuous months
options.rationale: A line shows change over time, not a comparison across genres.

options.text: A filled map with `Genre` on Detail
options.rationale: A filled map needs a geographic field, and `Genre` has no geographic role.

explanation: Use a bar chart when you compare a measure across the members of a dimension. Sorting the dimension by the measure makes the ranking easy to read.

stem: The Automatic mark type shows a Bar when which fields are the inner fields on Rows and Columns?

options.text: A date field and a measure
options.rationale: That combination makes Automatic choose Line.

options.text: A measure on each shelf
options.rationale: Two measures make a scatterplot, not bars.

options.text: `Longitude (generated)` and `Latitude (generated)`
options.rationale: Generated coordinates make a map, not bars.

options.text: A dimension and a measure
options.rationale: Automatic chooses Bar for a dimension and a measure as the inner fields.

explanation: Mark type Automatic reads the fields and chooses for you: Bar for a dimension plus a measure, Line for a date plus a measure. You only change the mark type when you want something else.

stem: On a view, `Plan` is on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` is on Rows. What does Automatic draw?

options.text: Horizontal bars, one per plan
options.rationale: Horizontal bars need the dimension on Rows and the measure on Columns.

options.text: Vertical bars, one per plan
options.rationale: A dimension on Columns with a measure on Rows grows bars upward.

options.text: A single line across the plan headers
options.rationale: Line is chosen for a date and a measure, and `Plan` is not a date.

options.text: A single mark for all plans
options.rationale: One mark would appear only with no dimension in the view.

explanation: The shelf of the dimension sets the bar direction. A dimension on Columns and a measure on Rows gives vertical bars; swapping them gives horizontal bars.

stem: An analyst wants horizontal bars of `Minutes Watched` per `Genre`. Which two steps build them? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag `Genre` to Rows
options.rationale: The dimension on Rows gives one horizontal bar per genre.

options.text: Drag `Genre` to Detail and `Minutes Watched` to Size
options.rationale: This draws marks sized by the measure, not bars along an axis.

options.text: Change the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density is for clusters of points on a map.

options.text: Drag `Minutes Watched` to Columns
options.rationale: The measure on Columns provides the axis the bars extend along.

options.text: Right-click `Minutes Watched` and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: Dual Axis layers two measures; it is not needed for a bar chart.

explanation: For a bar chart place a dimension on one shelf and a measure on the other. With the dimension on Rows and the measure on Columns the bars are horizontal.

stem: Which two statements about building a bar chart are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A bar chart needs two measures
options.rationale: Two measures make a scatterplot.

options.text: A dimension on Rows and a measure on Columns works, and so does the reverse
options.rationale: Either arrangement makes bars; only the direction changes.

options.text: Automatic never picks Bar; the mark type must be set by hand
options.rationale: Bar is one of the marks Automatic picks.

options.text: A date field must be on Columns
options.rationale: A date with a measure makes a line under Automatic.

options.text: Automatic can choose Bar from a dimension and a measure as inner fields
options.rationale: Automatic picks Bar for that field combination, so no manual mark choice is needed.

explanation: A bar chart is a recipe of one dimension and one measure. Automatic recognises it and draws bars.

stem: Which fields make Automatic draw a line chart?

options.text: `Start` on Columns and `Minutes Watched` on Rows
options.rationale: A date with a measure as the inner fields gives Line.

options.text: `Genre` on Columns and `Minutes Watched` on Rows
options.rationale: A dimension that is not a date gives bars.

options.text: `Plan` on Rows and `Device` on Columns
options.rationale: Two dimensions give a table of headers.

options.text: `Sessions (Count)` on Columns and `Minutes Watched` on Rows
options.rationale: Two measures give a scatterplot.

explanation: Line is the mark Automatic chooses when a date field and a measure are the inner fields. The date normally goes on Columns and the measure on Rows.

stem: An analyst drops the discrete date part `YEAR(Start)` on Columns with `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows. What does the view show?

options.text: A continuous time axis with one smooth line
options.rationale: A continuous axis needs a continuous date value.

options.text: Bars, because the date is discrete
options.rationale: Automatic still chooses Line for a date and a measure.

options.text: Headers for each year, with the line running across them
options.rationale: A discrete date part creates headers rather than an axis, and the line crosses the headers.

options.text: One separate chart for each year
options.rationale: The discrete part draws headers for the line to run across, not separate charts.

explanation: Discrete dates draw blue headers; continuous dates draw a green axis. The mark type stays Line either way, but the look differs.

stem: Which Driftlight question is best answered by a line chart?

options.text: Which titles are watched often but briefly?
options.rationale: Comparing two measures per title calls for a scatterplot.

options.text: How does each plan split by device?
options.rationale: A split into parts per bar suits a stacked bar.

options.text: Where are subscribers located?
options.rationale: Locations are shown on a map.

options.text: Is viewing growing from month to month?
options.rationale: A line shows how a measure changes along a continuous time axis.

explanation: Use a line chart for a measure over time. A continuous date lets Tableau draw one line along a linear time axis.

stem: On a line chart, the date pill on Columns is a continuous month value. How is it drawn?

options.text: Blue, creating headers
options.rationale: Blue pills are discrete and draw headers.

options.text: Green, creating an axis
options.rationale: Continuous pills are green and draw an axis.

options.text: Green, creating headers
options.rationale: Headers come from discrete pills, which are blue.

options.text: Blue, creating an axis
options.rationale: Axes come from continuous pills, which are green.

explanation: Blue means discrete and draws headers; green means continuous and draws an axis. A continuous date draws a time axis, so the line is one unbroken line.

stem: Which two statements about a line chart on a continuous date are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Automatic chooses Line when a date and a measure are the inner fields
options.rationale: That is the rule Automatic follows.

options.text: It creates a header for each date part
options.rationale: Headers come from discrete date parts.

options.text: The mark type has to be set to Line by hand
options.rationale: Automatic already picks Line here.

options.text: It draws one line along a linear, continuous axis
options.rationale: Continuous dimensions use a continuous axis.

options.text: It needs two date fields
options.rationale: One date and one measure are enough.

explanation: A continuous date value, such as a month, gives an axis. With a measure, Automatic draws one line along it.

stem: Which two steps build a line chart of `Minutes Watched` over time? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Put `Sessions (Count)` on Columns
options.rationale: A measure on Columns would turn the view into a scatterplot.

options.text: Put `Minutes Watched` on Rows
options.rationale: The measure gives the vertical axis for the line.

options.text: Set the mark type to Map
options.rationale: Map needs geographic data.

options.text: Drag `Start` to Color
options.rationale: Color alone does not build a time axis.

options.text: Put the date `Start` on Columns as a continuous month
options.rationale: The continuous date provides the time axis.

explanation: A line chart is a date plus a measure. Put the date on Columns, the measure on Rows, and let Automatic choose Line.

stem: What does a scatterplot require?

options.text: A dimension on each of Rows and Columns
options.rationale: Two dimensions only produce headers.

options.text: A date on Columns and a measure on Rows
options.rationale: That is the recipe for a line chart.

options.text: At least one measure on Columns and at least one on Rows
options.rationale: A scatterplot compares measure against measure.

options.text: A geographic field on Detail and a measure on Color
options.rationale: That describes a filled map.

explanation: Scatterplots place measures on both axes. Each mark shows how the two measures relate for one member.

stem: A view has `Sessions (Count)` on Columns and `Minutes Watched` on Rows, and shows one mark. How do you get one mark per title?

options.text: Drag `Title` to Detail
options.rationale: Detail splits the aggregation per title without changing the axes.

options.text: Drag `Title` to Columns
options.rationale: A dimension on Columns creates panes, each with its own scatterplot.

options.text: Drag `Title` to Rows
options.rationale: A dimension on Rows creates panes, not more marks in one chart.

options.text: Change the mark type to Map
options.rationale: Map needs geographic fields.

explanation: Detail adds a dimension to the level of detail without adding headers. That gives one mark per member in a single chart.

stem: Which Driftlight question suits a scatterplot of `Sessions (Count)` against `Minutes Watched`?

options.text: Which genre has the most minutes?
options.rationale: Ranking a dimension by one measure suits a bar chart.

options.text: Which titles are watched often but briefly?
options.rationale: Comparing two measures per title is a scatterplot.

options.text: What was the monthly trend?
options.rationale: A trend over time suits a line chart.

options.text: Which countries have subscribers?
options.rationale: Countries suit a map.

explanation: Use a scatterplot to see how two measures relate and to spot outliers. A dimension on Detail provides one mark per member.

stem: `Minutes Watched` is on Columns and `Sessions (Count)` is on Rows, with no other fields. Why is there only one mark?

options.text: Scatterplots only show one mark unless the mark type is Circle
options.rationale: The mark type does not change how many marks appear.

options.text: `Sessions (Count)` is a dimension
options.rationale: It is a measure, which is why this is a scatterplot.

options.text: A scatterplot needs a date field to show more than one mark
options.rationale: Dates are not required.

options.text: Both measures are aggregated over all the data without a dimension
options.rationale: With nothing splitting the data, each measure is one total.

explanation: Marks are created per combination of dimension members in the view. With none, there is one combination, so one mark.

stem: A scatterplot shows one mark. Which two changes add marks to the same chart? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag a dimension to Columns
options.rationale: This creates panes rather than more points in one chart.

options.text: Drag a dimension such as `Title` to Detail
options.rationale: Detail makes one mark per member.

options.text: Right-click a measure and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: Dual Axis layers two measures; it adds no marks by member.

options.text: Drag a dimension such as `Plan` to Color
options.rationale: Color splits marks per member and colours them.

options.text: Change the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density is for dense point maps.

explanation: Detail and Color add dimensions to the level of detail inside the same pane. Dimensions on shelves create panes.

stem: Which two statements about building a scatterplot are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It needs at least one measure on Columns and one on Rows
options.rationale: This is the recipe from Tableau help.

options.text: It needs a date on Columns
options.rationale: Dates build a line chart.

options.text: The second measure has to go on Color
options.rationale: Measures go on the shelves.

options.text: Without other fields, both measures are aggregated over all the data into a single mark
options.rationale: No dimension splits the data.

options.text: A dimension on Rows adds marks within one pane
options.rationale: It adds panes.

explanation: A scatterplot is measure by measure; dimensions on Detail or Color add marks.

stem: Which fields does Tableau generate for a field with a geographic role such as `Country`?

options.text: `Latitude (generated)` and `Longitude (generated)`
options.rationale: These coordinates are what you place on the shelves to draw a map.

options.text: `Latitude` and `Longitude` columns added to the data file
options.rationale: Tableau does not change the source; the generated fields exist only in the workbook.

options.text: A `Number of Records` measure
options.rationale: That counts rows and has nothing to do with location.

options.text: A second `Country` dimension on Color
options.rationale: No such field is created.

explanation: A geographic role lets Tableau place locations. It gives you generated latitude and longitude fields that you put on Columns and Rows.

stem: Where does an analyst select the Map mark type for a filled map?

options.text: In the Map menu under Background Maps
options.rationale: That menu sets the background map layers, not the mark type.

options.text: In the mark type drop-down on the Marks card
options.rationale: The Map mark type is chosen from the Marks card drop-down.

options.text: In the Analysis menu under Stack Marks
options.rationale: Stack Marks controls stacking of bars.

options.text: In the Format menu under Borders
options.rationale: Borders format view lines.

explanation: Filled maps use the Map mark type, selected from the mark type drop-down on the Marks card.

stem: A symbol map shows one circle per city. What turns it into a proportional symbol map?

options.text: Changing the mark type to Map
options.rationale: Map would fill areas instead.

options.text: Changing the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density shows clusters of points.

options.text: Dragging a measure to Size
options.rationale: A measure on Size scales each symbol.

options.text: Moving `City` from Detail to Rows
options.rationale: `City` would then create headers, and the map would break.

explanation: A symbol map places a mark per location. A measure on Size makes the symbols proportional to it.

stem: Which combination makes a filled map of `State` coloured by `Profit`?

options.text: Circle mark type, `State` on Detail, `Profit` on Size
options.rationale: That is a proportional symbol map.

options.text: Map mark type, `Profit` on Detail, `State` on Size
options.rationale: The geographic field belongs on Detail and the measure on Color.

options.text: Density mark type, `State` on Color, `Profit` on Detail
options.rationale: Density is not for filled areas.

options.text: Map mark type, `State` on Detail, `Profit` on Color
options.rationale: This is the filled map recipe.

explanation: A filled map needs the Map mark type, a geographic dimension on Detail and a measure on Color.

stem: The board wants each country shaded by its subscribers. Which map?

options.text: A filled map
options.rationale: Filled maps shade areas by a measure on Color.

options.text: A proportional symbol map of cities
options.rationale: It draws symbols sized by a measure, not shaded areas.

options.text: A scatterplot of `Latitude` against `Longitude`
options.rationale: It shows locations as points.

options.text: A line chart by `Country`
options.rationale: A line needs a date.

explanation: Use a filled map to shade areas by a measure, and a symbol map for marks per location.

stem: Which three steps build a symbol map of `City`? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Set the mark type to Map
options.rationale: Map is for filled maps.

options.text: Put `Longitude (generated)` on Columns
options.rationale: Longitude is the horizontal position.

options.text: Set the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density shows clusters, not one symbol per city.

options.text: Put `Latitude (generated)` on Rows
options.rationale: Latitude is the vertical position.

options.text: Put `City` on Detail
options.rationale: Detail makes one mark per city.

explanation: A symbol map needs generated coordinates on the shelves and a geographic field on Detail.

stem: Target Hours and Actual Hours must share one axis so they can be compared directly. What creates this combined axis chart?

options.text: Drag the second measure to the right side of the view until a black dashed line appears
options.rationale: That gesture creates a second axis, which is a dual axis.

options.text: Put both measures on Rows, then right-click one of them and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: Dual Axis gives each measure its own axis, so the axis is not shared.

options.text: Drag one measure or axis and drop it onto the existing axis
options.rationale: Dropping onto an existing axis blends the measures into one shared axis.

options.text: Drag the second measure to Color on the Marks card
options.rationale: A measure on Color shades marks; it does not put two measures on one axis.

explanation: A combined axis, called a blended axis in Tableau help, is made by dropping one measure or axis onto an existing axis. The measures then share one axis and can be compared directly.

stem: In a combined axis chart, which field is on Color so that each measure gets its own colour?

options.text: `Measure Names`
options.rationale: Tableau adds Measure Names to Color when measures are blended, one colour per measure.

options.text: `Measure Values`
options.rationale: Measure Values replaces the measures on the axis shelf; it is not the field on Color.

options.text: `Genre`
options.rationale: A dimension on Color would split the marks by genre instead of telling the measures apart.

options.text: `Sessions (Count)`
options.rationale: This is one of the measures, and it is merged into Measure Values rather than placed on Color.

explanation: Blending replaces the measures on the shelf with Measure Values and adds Measure Names to Color. The colours then say which measure each mark shows.

stem: Which pair of measures is the best candidate for a combined axis?

options.text: `Minutes Watched` in millions and `Sessions (Count)` in thousands
options.rationale: The scales differ a lot, so a dual axis suits these better.

options.text: `Monthly Price` in currency and `Runtime` in minutes
options.rationale: Different units belong on separate axes, as in a dual axis.

options.text: `Genre` and `Minutes Watched`
options.rationale: `Genre` is a dimension, and only measures are blended onto an axis.

options.text: Target Hours and Actual Hours, both measured in hours
options.rationale: Measures in the same units can share one axis and be compared directly.

explanation: Use a combined axis for measures in the same units, because one shared axis lets the reader compare them directly. Use a dual axis when the units or scales differ.

stem: Which two statements about a combined axis chart are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Both measures share a single axis
options.rationale: That is what makes the axis combined, or blended.

options.text: Each measure can have its own mark type
options.rationale: Separate mark types per measure belong to a dual axis; a combined axis has one.

options.text: `Measure Names` on Color tells the measures apart
options.rationale: Each measure gets its own colour through Measure Names.

options.text: It is the better choice when the measures have very different scales
options.rationale: A shared axis would squash the smaller measure; a dual axis suits different scales.

options.text: It is created with the Dual Axis command
options.rationale: Dual Axis creates two axes, not a shared one.

explanation: A combined axis puts several measures on one shared axis, with Measure Names on Color to distinguish them. It has one set of marks, so it suits measures in the same units.

stem: A chart shows Target Hours and Actual Hours on one shared axis, coloured by `Measure Names`. Which two statements describe how it was built? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The analyst chose Dual Axis from the pill menu
options.rationale: That would have produced two axes.

options.text: One measure was dropped onto the axis of the other
options.rationale: Dropping a measure onto an existing axis is how the axis is blended.

options.text: `Measure Values` replaced the individual measures on the shelf
options.rationale: Blending swaps the measures for Measure Values.

options.text: Synchronize Axis was applied to the secondary axis
options.rationale: Synchronize Axis aligns two axes; this chart has only one.

options.text: A second Marks card was added for the new measure
options.rationale: A Marks card per measure appears with a dual axis, not with a blended axis.

explanation: To blend measures, drag one measure or axis and drop it onto an existing axis. Tableau then uses Measure Values on the shelf and Measure Names on Color.

stem: `Minutes Watched` and `Sessions (Count)` are both on Rows. Which right-click command on one of the pills makes a dual axis chart?

options.text: Synchronize Axis
options.rationale: That command sets the two axes to the same scale after a dual axis exists.

options.text: Dual Axis
options.rationale: Choosing Dual Axis layers the two measures, each with its own axis.

options.text: Edit Axis
options.rationale: This changes the range or title of an axis, not the number of axes.

options.text: Add Reference Line
options.rationale: A reference line is an overlay on one axis; it does not layer a second measure.

explanation: Put both measures on Rows or Columns, then right-click one and select Dual Axis. Tableau layers the measures with an axis on each side.

stem: The two axes of a dual axis chart have different ranges. How does the analyst put them on the same scale?

options.text: Drag one measure onto the other axis to blend them
options.rationale: Blending replaces the dual axis with one combined axis rather than aligning the two.

options.text: Set Stack Marks to Off in the Analysis menu
options.rationale: Stack Marks controls stacking, which has no effect on axis scales.

options.text: Change the mark type on the second Marks card
options.rationale: Mark types change the drawing, not the axis range.

options.text: Right-click the secondary axis and select Synchronize Axis
options.rationale: Synchronize Axis makes both axes use the same range.

explanation: The two axes of a dual axis chart are independent. To put them on the same scale, right-click the secondary axis and select Synchronize Axis.

stem: What lets a dual axis chart show bars for `Minutes Watched` and a line for `Sessions (Count)`?

options.text: Each measure has its own Marks card, so each can have its own mark type
options.rationale: This is why bars and a line can be combined in one chart.

options.text: `Measure Names` on Color assigns a mark type to each measure
options.rationale: Measure Names only colours; mark types are set on Marks cards.

options.text: Synchronize Axis lets the two axes draw different mark types
options.rationale: Synchronizing aligns the scales but has no effect on mark types.

options.text: Automatic always draws the second measure as a line
options.rationale: Automatic follows the fields in the view and doesn't apply a fixed rule for second measures.

explanation: A dual axis chart has a Marks card for each measure, so you can set each measure's mark type independently. Bars for one measure and a line for the other is the classic combo chart.

stem: Which two situations call for a dual axis rather than a combined axis? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Minutes watched in millions shown next to sessions in thousands
options.rationale: The scales differ, so each measure needs its own axis.

options.text: Target Hours and Actual Hours, both in hours
options.rationale: Same units suit a shared, combined axis.

options.text: A combo chart with bars for one measure and a line for another
options.rationale: Only a dual axis offers a mark type per measure.

options.text: Two measures that must share one axis and one mark type
options.rationale: That describes a combined axis.

options.text: A bar split into coloured segments by a dimension
options.rationale: That is a stacked bar, made with a dimension on Color.

explanation: A dual axis suits measures with different units or scales, and it allows a different mark type per measure. A combined axis suits measures in the same units on one shared axis.

stem: Which two statements about building a dual axis chart are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The second measure can be dropped on the right side of the view when a black dashed line appears
options.rationale: That gesture creates the second axis.

options.text: Both measures must use the same mark type
options.rationale: Each measure has its own Marks card and mark type.

options.text: `Measure Names` is placed on Color automatically
options.rationale: That happens when axes are blended, not in a dual axis.

options.text: Up to four layered axes are possible, two on Columns and two on Rows
options.rationale: Tableau help states this limit.

options.text: Synchronize Axis has to be applied before the second axis appears
options.rationale: Synchronizing is an optional step after both axes exist.

explanation: A dual axis can be made by dropping a measure on the right side of the view or by choosing Dual Axis on a pill. Tableau allows up to four layered axes: two on Columns and two on Rows.

stem: A bar chart shows `Minutes Watched` by `Plan`. How does the analyst split each bar into device segments?

options.text: Drag `Device` to Columns next to `Plan`
options.rationale: A dimension on Columns adds a second level of headers, not segments inside one bar.

options.text: Right-click `Minutes Watched` and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: Dual Axis layers two measures; it does not split a bar by a dimension.

options.text: Drag `Device` to Color
options.rationale: A dimension on Color stacks the bar into one segment per member.

options.text: Change the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density draws clusters of points on a map, not stacked bars.

explanation: A stacked bar is a bar chart with a second dimension on Color. Tableau stacks the marks automatically, so each bar splits into segments that add up to its total.

stem: Which menu controls whether marks are stacked, and what is its default setting?

options.text: Format > Stack Marks, with a default of On
options.rationale: Stack Marks is in the Analysis menu, and the default isn't On.

options.text: Analysis > Stack Marks, with a default of Automatic
options.rationale: Stack Marks offers Automatic, On and Off, and Automatic is the default.

options.text: Map > Stack Marks, with a default of Off
options.rationale: The Map menu holds map settings, and the default isn't Off.

options.text: Data > Stack Marks, with a default of Automatic
options.rationale: The setting is in the Analysis menu, not the Data menu.

explanation: Analysis > Stack Marks lets Tableau decide whether to stack automatically, or you can specify On or Off. The default setting is Automatic.

stem: Which Driftlight question is best answered by a stacked bar?

options.text: How does each plan's viewing split by device?
options.rationale: Segments by a second dimension within each bar are a stacked bar.

options.text: Where are subscribers clustered?
options.rationale: Clusters of points are shown on a density map.

options.text: What are the exact minutes for each region and year?
options.rationale: Exact values call for a crosstab.

options.text: How do minutes and sessions compare in one chart?
options.rationale: Two measures with different scales suit a dual axis.

explanation: Use a stacked bar to show how each bar's total splits among the members of another dimension. Here, each plan's bar is split by device.

stem: A bar chart has `Device` on Color but the bars are not stacked. How can the analyst force stacking?

options.text: Right-click an axis and select Synchronize Axis
options.rationale: Synchronize Axis aligns two axes and has no effect on stacking.

options.text: Change the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density is for clusters on maps.

options.text: Move `Device` from Color to Rows
options.rationale: `Device` on Rows creates headers, not stacked segments.

options.text: Choose Analysis > Stack Marks > On
options.rationale: The Stack Marks setting can be set to On instead of Automatic.

explanation: Stacking is governed by Analysis > Stack Marks. Automatic is the default, but On and Off can be specified.

stem: Which two steps build a stacked bar of `Minutes Watched` by `Plan` split by `Device`? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Set the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density is for clusters of points.

options.text: Build a bar chart with `Plan` and `Minutes Watched` on the shelves
options.rationale: A stacked bar starts as an ordinary bar chart.

options.text: Right-click `Minutes Watched` and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: Dual Axis layers two measures; it is not needed here.

options.text: Drag `Device` to Color
options.rationale: The second dimension on Color splits each bar into segments.

options.text: Set the mark type to Square
options.rationale: Square is part of a highlight table.

explanation: Start with a bar chart and drag a second dimension to Color. Tableau stacks the marks automatically.

stem: Where does the analyst choose the Density mark type?

options.text: In the Analysis menu under Stack Marks
options.rationale: Stack Marks controls stacking, not the mark type.

options.text: In the mark type drop-down on the Marks card, next to Automatic
options.rationale: The Density mark type is chosen from this drop-down.

options.text: In the Map menu under Map Layers
options.rationale: Map Layers set background layers, not the mark type.

options.text: On the Intensity slider
options.rationale: The slider adjusts vividness once Density is selected.

explanation: A density map uses the Density mark type. Open the mark type drop-down on the Marks card, to the right of Automatic, and select Density.

stem: A density map of subscribers has `Longitude` on Columns, `Latitude` on Rows and the Density mark. Which field on Detail provides many underlying points?

options.text: `Country`
options.rationale: One mark per country gives too few points for clusters to show.

options.text: `Region`
options.rationale: One mark per region gives too few points for clusters to show.

options.text: `Subscriber ID`
options.rationale: An ID has one value per subscriber, so there are many points to cluster.

options.text: `Device`
options.rationale: `Device` isn't unique per subscriber and has few members.

explanation: A density map needs a field on Detail with many underlying data points, such as an ID. The Density mark then shows where those points cluster.

stem: What does the Intensity slider do on a density map?

options.text: It increases or decreases the vividness of the map
options.rationale: Intensity controls how vivid the density colours look.

options.text: It selects one of ten density colour palettes
options.rationale: Palettes are chosen separately in the Color settings.

options.text: It sets the number of points drawn
options.rationale: Points come from the field on Detail, not from the slider.

options.text: It switches the mark type between Density and Map
options.rationale: Mark types are chosen from the Marks card drop-down.

explanation: Tableau offers ten density colour palettes and an Intensity slider that increases or decreases the vividness of the map. Size adjusts the mark size.

stem: Subscribers are drawn as individual points and many overlap. Which map shows where they cluster?

options.text: A filled map coloured by subscribers
options.rationale: It shades whole areas and shows no clustering inside them.

options.text: A symbol map with `City` on Detail
options.rationale: It draws one circle per location, and overlapping circles hide clusters.

options.text: A line chart by `Country`
options.rationale: A line needs a date and doesn't show locations.

options.text: A density map
options.rationale: The Density mark reveals where many points cluster.

explanation: Use a density map for data with many overlapping points. The Density mark turns clusters into visible colour intensity.

stem: Which three steps build a density map of subscribers? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Put `Longitude` on Columns and `Latitude` on Rows
options.rationale: The coordinates give each point its position.

options.text: Set the mark type to Map and put a measure on Color
options.rationale: That is a filled map, not a density map.

options.text: Put `Subscriber ID` on Detail
options.rationale: A field with many data points gives the Density mark points to cluster.

options.text: Set the mark type to Density
options.rationale: The Density mark draws clusters instead of individual marks.

options.text: Right-click `Latitude` and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: Dual Axis is not part of the density recipe.

explanation: A density map needs the coordinates on Columns and Rows, a field with many data points on Detail, and the Density mark type.

stem: A crosstab has `Region` on Rows and `YEAR(Start)` on Columns. Where should the analyst drag `SUM(Minutes Watched)` to show the numbers in the cells?

options.text: Size on the Marks card
options.rationale: Size scales the marks and doesn't print values.

options.text: Text on the Marks card
options.rationale: Text prints the measure's value in each cell of the table.

options.text: Detail on the Marks card
options.rationale: Detail only adds a level of detail.

options.text: Rows, to the right of `Region`
options.rationale: A measure on Rows draws an axis, which turns the table into a chart.

explanation: A crosstab (text table) has one dimension on Rows, another on Columns and one or more measures on Text on the Marks card.

stem: Which mark type does a highlight table use?

options.text: Text
options.rationale: Text is the mark type of a crosstab.

options.text: Bar
options.rationale: Bar draws bars along an axis, not filled cells.

options.text: Square
options.rationale: Square marks fill the cells, and a measure on Color shades them.

options.text: Density
options.rationale: Density draws clusters of points.

explanation: A highlight table places dimensions on Columns and Rows, selects Square as the mark type and puts a measure of interest on Color.

stem: In a crosstab with the measure on Text, the analyst also drags the measure to Color and leaves the mark type as Text. What is the result?

options.text: The numbers are coloured, but it is not a highlight table
options.rationale: Color alone only colours the numbers.

options.text: A highlight table, because Color is all it needs
options.rationale: A highlight table also needs the Square mark type.

options.text: Tableau switches the mark type to Square automatically
options.rationale: The mark type stays Text unless the analyst changes it.

options.text: A dual axis chart with two Marks cards
options.rationale: Dual Axis comes from a right-click command on a measure pill.

explanation: A crosstab puts the measure on Text. A highlight table changes the mark type to Square and puts the measure on Color. Color alone with Text only colours the numbers.

stem: Finance needs the exact minutes for every region and year in one view. Which chart fits best?

options.text: A dual axis chart
options.rationale: It layers two measures and is read from axes, not from exact cell values.

options.text: A crosstab
options.rationale: A crosstab shows exact values in a table of dimensions by dimensions.

options.text: A density map
options.rationale: It shows clusters of points, not exact values.

options.text: A stacked bar
options.rationale: It shows segments, which are harder to read as exact values.

explanation: Use a table when readers need exact numbers rather than shapes. A crosstab can be upgraded to a highlight table when the big cells should stand out.

stem: Which three steps build a highlight table of `Region` by `YEAR(Start)`? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Set the mark type to Density
options.rationale: Density is for clusters of points.

options.text: Put `Region` on Rows and `YEAR(Start)` on Columns
options.rationale: A highlight table has dimensions on both shelves.

options.text: Set the mark type to Square
options.rationale: Square is the mark type of a highlight table.

options.text: Right-click the measure and choose Dual Axis
options.rationale: A dual axis layers measures on axes; there are no axes in this table.

options.text: Put the measure on Color
options.rationale: The measure on Color shades the squares.

explanation: A highlight table has dimensions on Rows and Columns, the Square mark type and a measure on Color. Keeping the measure on Label too shows the exact value.

stem: The chart ranks genres by total minutes, longest bar at the top. Which setup produces it?

options.text: `Genre` on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows, with `Genre` sorted descending by `SUM(Minutes Watched)`.
options.rationale: A dimension on Columns with the measure on Rows draws vertical bars, but these bars run horizontally.

options.text: `Genre` on Rows and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Columns, with `Genre` sorted descending by `SUM(Minutes Watched)`.
options.rationale: The dimension on Rows with the measure on Columns gives horizontal bars, and the computed sort ranks them by length.

options.text: `Genre` on Rows and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Columns, with `Genre` left on its default alphabetical order.
options.rationale: The orientation is right, but the default order would list genres alphabetically, not by bar length.

options.text: `Genre` on Rows and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Columns, with `Genre` also dragged to Color.
options.rationale: Color would paint each bar a different hue; it does not rank bars, and this chart is one colour.

explanation: A bar chart needs a dimension and a measure. Which shelf holds the dimension sets the direction: dimension on Rows gives horizontal bars. The order of the bars comes from the dimension's sort, which can be computed from the measure.

stem: Look at the shelves. Which view will Tableau draw with the mark type left on Automatic?

options.text: A single bar, because `Subscribers (Count)` is aggregated over all plans.
options.rationale: `Plan` is a dimension in the view, so the measure is split per plan, not totalled into one mark.

options.text: A line across the plans, because the measure is continuous.
options.rationale: Automatic draws a line only when a date is an inner field; `Plan` is not a date.

options.text: Horizontal bars, one per `Plan`.
options.rationale: A dimension on Rows with a measure on Columns gives Automatic a Bar mark, with the bars running left to right.

options.text: Vertical bars, one per `Plan`.
options.rationale: Vertical bars need the dimension on Columns and the measure on Rows. Here the shelves are the other way round.

explanation: With a dimension and a measure as the inner fields, Automatic chooses Bar. The measure's shelf sets the bar length direction: a measure on Columns means horizontal bars.

stem: Which two questions can this chart answer? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Which genre has the most total minutes watched?
options.rationale: The longest bar is the genre with the largest `SUM(Minutes Watched)`.

options.text: How does `Minutes Watched` in `Drama` compare with `Minutes Watched` in `Comedy`?
options.rationale: Bars share one axis, so comparing two genres means comparing two bar lengths.

options.text: Did total minutes watched rise or fall from month to month?
options.rationale: There is no date on the view, so it carries no information about change over time.

options.text: Which device was used most in each genre?
options.rationale: `Device` is not on the view, so the bars cannot show a device split.

options.text: How are `Minutes Watched` and `Sessions (Count)` related across titles?
options.rationale: That is a measure against a measure, which takes a scatterplot with one mark per title.

explanation: A bar chart of one measure by one dimension compares categories. It shows the ranking and the size of the gaps, but only for the fields on the view; time or another split would need another field.

stem: In this bar chart, the device names are listed down the left as headers while the bottom shows a numeric scale. Why?

options.text: `Device` is a measure, so it draws headers, and `AVG(Minutes Watched)` is a dimension, so it draws an axis.
options.rationale: The roles are reversed: `Device` is the dimension and the average is the measure.

options.text: Every bar chart shows headers on Rows and an axis on Columns, whichever fields are used.
options.rationale: Headers or axes depend on whether a pill is discrete or continuous, not on its shelf.

options.text: The `AVG` aggregation turns the measure into a header that Tableau labels with a scale.
options.rationale: Aggregation does not create headers. It only fixes how rows combine, and the pill stays continuous.

options.text: `Device` is discrete, so it draws headers, and `AVG(Minutes Watched)` is continuous, so it draws an axis.
options.rationale: Blue discrete pills create headers; green continuous pills create axes.

explanation: Discrete (blue) pills slice the view and add headers. Continuous (green) pills add an axis. In a bar chart the dimension supplies the headers and the measure supplies the axis.

stem: With `Genre` and `Device` on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows, what does Automatic draw?

options.text: One bar per `Genre`, with the devices stacked inside each bar.
options.rationale: Stacking needs a dimension on Color. Dimensions on Columns add headers instead.

options.text: A bar for every `Genre` and `Device` combination, grouped under the genre headers.
options.rationale: With a dimension and a measure as inner fields, Automatic draws bars, and the extra dimension adds one bar per member within each header.

options.text: One line per `Device`, running across the genres.
options.rationale: Automatic draws a line only for a date field, and `Genre` is not one.

options.text: A single bar showing the total minutes of all sessions.
options.rationale: Both dimensions are in the view, so the measure is split by them and not totalled.

explanation: Each dimension on a shelf slices the data further. The view has one mark per combination of its dimension members, and with a dimension and a measure as inner fields, Automatic draws them as bars.

stem: The chart is one line along a time axis, with a mark for every month of 2024 and 2025. Which setup produces it?

options.text: Discrete `MONTH(Start)` on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows.
options.rationale: A discrete month part would draw 12 headers, January to December, with both years merged.

options.text: Discrete `YEAR(Start)` on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows.
options.rationale: A discrete year gives only two headers, so there would be two marks, not 24.

options.text: `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Columns and continuous `MONTH(Start)` on Rows.
options.rationale: That puts time on the vertical axis, so the line would run from top to bottom.

options.text: Continuous `MONTH(Start)` on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows.
options.rationale: A continuous month value draws a time axis, and a mark for each month in the range makes one long line.

explanation: A line chart needs a date and a measure. A continuous date value gives a linear time axis, so every month in the range becomes a point. A discrete date part gives headers and groups months across years.

stem: Look at the shelves. What does one mark in this view stand for?

options.text: The total minutes in one month of one specific year, so the view has 24 marks.
options.rationale: That is what a continuous month value gives. A month part carries no year.

options.text: The minutes of a single session that started in that month.
options.rationale: The measure is aggregated, so each mark combines many sessions.

options.text: The total minutes in one calendar month, with 2024 and 2025 added together.
options.rationale: A discrete month part groups by month name only, so the same month of both years falls into one mark.

options.text: The average minutes per session across all months.
options.rationale: The aggregation is `SUM`, and the marks are split by month, not totalled into one.

explanation: A date part such as `MONTH(Start)` keeps only the month, so months of different years merge. A date value keeps the full date, one point per month in the range. This choice decides what each mark means.

stem: The line chart has one line per device. Which two statements explain the view? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `Device` on Color splits the line into one line per device member.
options.rationale: A dimension on Color breaks the marks into a separate line for each member.

options.text: The `Start` pill is a continuous date value, so Tableau draws a time axis.
options.rationale: A green date pill draws an axis, and a mark per month makes the line.

options.text: `Device` is a measure, which is why it is drawn as several lines.
options.rationale: `Device` is a dimension. Measures add values, not groups.

options.text: The lines would merge into one if `Device` were removed from Color and the pill moved to the Filters shelf.
options.rationale: A filter only limits which devices appear; it does not draw them as separate lines.

options.text: The `Start` pill is discrete, so every month appears as its own header.
options.rationale: The pill is green. A discrete part would show headers, not a continuous axis.

explanation: The date on Columns decides the axis and the line, and the dimension on Color decides how many lines are drawn. Together they answer how a measure changes over time for each member.

stem: The chart plots `SUM(Sessions (Count))` against a continuous quarter. Which question does it answer?

options.text: Which device had the most sessions in each quarter?
options.rationale: `Device` is not on the view, so no split by device appears.

options.text: Is the number of sessions growing from one quarter to the next?
options.rationale: A line across quarters shows how the session count changes over time.

options.text: What share of all sessions does each genre account for?
options.rationale: A share by genre needs a genre on the view, and a line over time is not a part-to-whole view.

options.text: Which single session ran the longest?
options.rationale: The measure counts sessions. It says nothing about the length of one session.

explanation: A line chart answers questions about change over time. Here the measure is a count of sessions and the date is continuous quarters, so the trend of volume is the story.

stem: Look at the shelves. Which two statements about this view are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Each mark is the average `Minutes Watched` of the sessions that started in one month.
options.rationale: The `AVG` pill averages the rows within each month on the axis.

options.text: The marks are joined in date order because the month pill is continuous.
options.rationale: With a continuous date and a measure, Automatic draws a line that connects the points along the time axis.

options.text: Each mark is the total minutes of the month, because measures are always summed.
options.rationale: The aggregation is on the pill. This one is `AVG`, not `SUM`.

options.text: Tableau draws one mark per session, so the line has thousands of points.
options.rationale: The measure is aggregated per month, which gives one mark per month.

options.text: The month pill is discrete, so Tableau draws headers and no line.
options.rationale: The pill is green and continuous, which gives an axis and a line.

explanation: The date pill decides the shape and the aggregation decides what each point means. A continuous date with an aggregated measure gives one point per month, joined into a line.
